summary: Describes a framework for using forward error correction codes with applications in IP networks to protect against packet loss. It supports applying FEC to arbitrary packet flows over unreliable transport, mainly for real-time or streaming media.

plainLanguage.summary: Send a few extra clue packets with your video, and if some get lost the receiver can fill in the gaps. This framework describes how to add such extras to any stream of packets.

questions: how does fec recover lost packets
subtitle: A common frame that lets any streaming protocol use any FEC code to survive packet loss.

tldr.problem: Real-time and streaming media travel over networks that do not guarantee delivery, and every protocol that wants forward error correction would otherwise need its own custom FEC design.
tldr.mechanism: The FEC Framework adds a thin layer between the transport and the application. It groups application data units into source blocks, hands them to a pluggable FEC scheme that produces repair packets, and sends source and repair packets as separate flows.
tldr.outcome: Content delivery protocols and FEC schemes can be specified independently and combined freely. The framework is not meant to fix congestion: repair traffic must not exceed the protected data, and it must shrink when the source rate shrinks.

today: RFC 6363 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 8680. Its companion for session descriptions is RFC 6364.

sections.title: Why a Framework for FEC
sections.content:
Many applications send a continuous stream of packets from a sender to one or more receivers over networks that do not guarantee delivery. Streaming audio, video and multimedia, whether broadcast, multicast or on demand, are the main examples.

Forward Error Correction (FEC) improves reliability by sending extra encoded data along with the original data so the receiver can rebuild lost packets without asking for a resend. The RFC points out that it deals strictly with erasures: losses that can be detected, as opposed to packets that arrive corrupted.

The earlier FEC Building Block (RFC 5052) covers object and file delivery. This document does the same job for arbitrary packet flows over unreliable transports such as UDP. It defines only what every Content Delivery Protocol (CDP) built on it would share, not a complete protocol. How flows are chosen and how settings reach the receiver are left to each CDP.
sections.plainLanguage: Some packets get lost on the way. Sending a few extra helper packets lets the receiver fix the gaps without calling the sender, and this memo describes a shared recipe for doing that.

sections.title: Architecture and Building Blocks
sections.content:
The framework sits as an extra layer between the transport layer (for example UDP or DCCP) and the protocols above it. Its data path looks like the ordinary transport interface: datagram payloads, each tied to one ADU flow identified by the usual 5-tuple of addresses, ports and protocol.

The real encoding and decoding work is done by a FEC scheme. The interface between the framework and a scheme exists only for specification purposes. At the sender the framework passes application data units (ADUs) to the scheme and gets back repair symbols with their Repair FEC Payload IDs and, for some schemes, Source FEC Payload IDs. At the receiver it passes received source and repair payloads in and gets recovered source payloads back.

The main goal is to divide responsibilities among separately documented components so they can be combined in different ways. RTP is optional on both sides: source flows can be RTP, and repair flows can use RTP as well, in which case the FEC scheme must define an RTP payload format. The two uses are independent of each other. If the source is RTP, the scheme is expected to recover the whole UDP payload, RTP header included.
sections.plainLanguage: The framework is a mail room in the middle. It does not know how to make clue cards itself. It passes the parcels to a specialist (the FEC scheme) and sends out whatever the specialist hands back.

sections.title: How Sender and Receiver Work
sections.content:
At the sender, ADUs from the application are gathered into a source block, which is an ordered sequence of ADUs. For each ADU the framework provides a description of its source flow, the ADU itself and its length. The block goes to the FEC scheme, which returns repair packet payloads, a Repair FEC Payload ID for each, and optionally Source FEC Payload IDs. The framework builds FEC source packets and FEC repair packets and sends them through normal transport procedures. Source packets keep the same ADU flow identification they would have had without FEC.

How ADUs are assigned to blocks, and the order and timing of sending, are not defined here. A CDP may define them or leave them to the implementation, but a CDP MUST define how a receiver works out the minimum time to wait for repair packets for a block.

At the receiver, original ADUs come straight out of the source packets by dropping any Source FEC Payload ID. The scheme uses the payload IDs to group packets into blocks. If at least one source packet of a block is missing and at least one repair packet for it has arrived, decoding can recover the missing payloads, provided enough data was received. Recovery can still fail, so not every ADU is guaranteed to come back.

Because repair packets can arrive late, a receiver may buffer source packets. Recovered packets MAY be delivered out of order, or buffered and put back in order if the application needs it.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender packs packets into small groups and makes helper packets for each group. The receiver collects each group. If one packet is missing and the helpers arrived, it works out the missing one.

sections.title: Source Packets, Repair Packets and Configuration
sections.content:
An FEC source packet carries the original ADU, optionally followed by an Explicit Source FEC Payload ID. The scheme decides whether that field is needed, and its format is defined by the scheme. If the scheme can derive the ID from something already in the packet, such as an application sequence number, the field is left out and the FEC source packet is identical to the original. The ID goes at the end so that header compression such as ROHC still applies. Adding it makes packets longer and can break backward compatibility with an existing protocol, so CDPs SHOULD allow for it when avoiding IP fragmentation.

An FEC repair packet carries a Repair FEC Payload ID followed by repair symbols. Over RTP, an RTP header comes first. The Repair FEC Payload ID is always an explicit field, defined by the scheme.

It is RECOMMENDED that schemes support a Generic Explicit Source FEC Payload ID: a two-octet unsigned sequence number in network byte order. Packets in one source block MUST have consecutive numbers, wrapping from 65535 to 0, so several schemes can protect the same flow.

The FEC Framework Configuration Information must be known to both ends, and a complete CDP MUST say how it is communicated. It contains the repair flow identification, each protected source flow with an integer identifier that is unique among the flows protected by the same repair flow, the FEC Encoding ID, the length of the Explicit Source FEC Payload ID, and zero or more FEC-Scheme-Specific Information (FSSI) elements. All packets on a protected source flow MUST be FEC source packets, and a repair flow carries only repair packets of one framework instance.
sections.plainLanguage: Each normal packet may get a small tag so the receiver knows which group it belongs to. Helper packets carry a tag too. Both sides also need the same instruction sheet saying which streams are protected and which scheme is used.

sections.title: What a FEC Scheme Must Provide
sections.content:
To work with the framework, a FEC scheme MUST handle data arranged as source blocks of ADUs. A specification for a new scheme MUST include:

  • a FEC Encoding ID that uniquely identifies it and is registered with IANA;
  • the type, semantics and encoding of the Repair FEC Payload ID;
  • the name, type, semantics and text encoding rules of any FSSI elements;
  • a full specification of the FEC code, precise enough to determine exactly which encoding symbols go into a repair packet;
  • a description of practical encoding and decoding algorithms, enough to show both are possible and practical.

A scheme MAY also define an Explicit Source FEC Payload ID. Any encoding format MUST have a fixed length or a length that can be derived from the encoded bytes. Schemes SHOULD follow a suggested outline (introduction, formats and codes, procedures, code specification) and each MUST be specified independently of the others.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone who invents a new way of making helper packets has to write down exactly how it works, give it a unique ID number, and show that it can really be done.

sections.title: Feedback and Congestion Control
sections.content:
FEC applies to small blocks sent over short periods, so feedback averaged over long periods is not enough for engineering purposes. Applications that use feedback for congestion control MUST compute it from packets received before FEC recovery, so that congestion control reacts to what the network did and not to repaired data. New applications that need feedback SHOULD use RTP/RTCP.

The framework is explicitly not a quality-of-service tool to fight losses from heavily congested networks and should not be used that way. Two rules apply to all compliant senders:

  • The bandwidth of FEC repair data MUST NOT exceed the bandwidth of the original source data (not counting any Explicit Source FEC Payload ID).
  • Whenever congestion control changes the source data rate, the repair data rate MUST be adapted in the same way.

The RFC admits a few exotic cases, such as traffic from space-based senders, could justify stronger FEC, but it gives preference to overall stability and network friendliness.
sections.plainLanguage: The extra helper packets must never be more than the real ones. If the sender slows down because the road is jammed, the helpers must slow down too, so the helpers do not make the jam worse.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC begins by saying FEC protection provides no security at all, and that the framework itself could be attacked. Attacks can target confidentiality, corrupt flows, make receivers waste effort decoding, or harm the network. They can aim at the data flows or at the FEC parameters.

For confidentiality, encryption MUST be applied either before FEC protection or, if after, to both source and repair packets with at least equal strength. Otherwise an unauthorized receiver could decode the source data from repair packets. Suggested tools are SRTP and IPsec/ESP.

For integrity and source authentication it is RECOMMENDED that at least one technique, such as SRTP (optionally with TESLA) or IPsec/ESP, be used, and that it cover both source and repair packets so corrupted packets stay out of decoding.

The Configuration Information and the payload IDs should also be integrity protected, because changing, for example, a source block number sends a packet to the wrong block. If configuration is sent out of band, such as in a session description, it SHOULD be protected, for instance by a digital signature. When flows with different security needs are protected together, the combined flow should meet the strictest requirement. A baseline secure mode based on IPsec/ESP is described by reference to RFC 5775 and RFC 5740.
sections.plainLanguage: Extra helper packets do not lock anything. If the stream is private, lock it before making helpers, or lock both. Anyone could also send fake packets, so check where packets come from.

sections.title: Operations and IANA
sections.content:
The framework is one small generic component inside a larger solution, and it works in very different settings: one-way broadcast with no feedback, or two-way setups with feedback; Internet or private networks such as IPTV; inside end systems or inside middleboxes. Because of this the RFC does not dictate how to manage hosts or signal configuration, but it gives SHOULD-level guidance.

  • Implementations SHOULD make feedback available through RTCP, and via an in-band or out-of-band asynchronous reporting mechanism; Syslog or SNMP notifications are RECOMMENDED for out-of-band reporting.
  • To stay compatible with receivers that do not understand FEC, avoid the Explicit Source FEC Payload ID and send repair packets on a different transport flow or, for RTP, with a different payload type.
  • Middleboxes doing FEC encoding or decoding should have paths to the end hosts that are as reliable as possible.
  • Receivers that want the benefit of a jointly protected bundle SHOULD receive all of its flows, and senders SHOULD send a bundle only to receivers authorized for all of it.

For IANA, the document creates the registry FEC Framework (FECFRAME) FEC Encoding IDs. Values are numeric indexes in the range (0, 255), values 0 and 255 are reserved, and assignments need IETF Review.
sections.plainLanguage: The framework works in many different setups, so it only gives advice. For example, keep helper packets on a separate path so devices that do not understand them can ignore them.
